## Important Caveat on Comparability

The source filings excerpted for this question (`airlines_costs_fy2024.txt`) provide only **total operating revenue, aircraft fuel expense, salaries/wages/benefits, and operating income** for each carrier — they do **not** include available seat miles (ASM) or total operating expense breakdowns needed to calculate a true unit-cost metric like CASM (cost per available seat mile), which is the standard industry measure of cost efficiency [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

Because true CASM figures aren't available in this corpus, I've used a **proxy measure — operating expense as a percentage of revenue (i.e., 100% minus operating margin)** — calculated from the disclosed revenue and operating income figures (Operating Expense = Revenue − Operating Income). This proxy is **not capacity-adjusted**, so it reflects each airline's overall cost-to-revenue efficiency rather than a true per-unit cost comparison, and results can be skewed by differences in average fare levels, stage length, and revenue mix across carriers.

Additionally, **Alaska Air Group's FY2024 results are not directly comparable** to the other four airlines because Alaska completed its acquisition of Hawaiian Holdings on September 18, 2024, and Hawaiian's results (which contributed a $113 million net loss on $869 million of revenue) are only included from that date forward — meaning Alaska's FY2024 figures reflect a partial-year, transitional combined entity rather than a full year of comparable stand-alone or fully-integrated operations [DOC: alaska_10k_note_acquisition.txt: "On September 18, 2024, Alaska Air Group completed its acquisition of Hawaiian Holdings, Inc... For the period from the acquisition date to December 31, 2024, revenue and net loss from Hawaiian recognized in the Company's consolidated results of operations was $869 million and $113 million, respectively."].

## Proxy Cost-Efficiency Comparison (Operating Expense / Revenue, FY2024)

| Airline | Revenue ($M) | Operating Income ($M) | Implied Op. Expense ($M) | Op. Expense / Revenue | Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Delta | 61,643 | 5,995 | 55,648 | **90.3%** | 9.7% |
| United | 57,063 | 5,096 | 51,967 | 91.1% | 8.9% |
| Alaska* | 11,735 | 570 | 11,165 | 95.1% | 4.9% |
| American | 54,211 | 2,614 | 51,597 | 95.2% | 4.8% |
| Southwest | 27,483 | 321 | 27,162 | 98.8% | 1.2% |

(*Alaska figures include partial-year Hawaiian results and are not fully comparable — see caveat above.)

Sources: [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt] — Delta (10-K accession 0000027904-25-000004), United (0000100517-25-000046), Southwest (0000092380-25-000024), American (0000006201-25-000010), Alaska (0000766421-25-000009).

## Conclusion

Based on this revenue-normalized cost proxy (since true CASM data was not available in the source excerpts), **Delta Air Lines** had the lowest operating expenses relative to revenue (90.3%) and the highest operating margin (9.7%) among the five carriers in FY2024, suggesting the most efficient cost structure by this measure. United was a close second. Southwest had by far the least efficient cost structure by this proxy (98.8% expense ratio, 1.2% margin), and American and Alaska were roughly comparable to each other in the middle — though Alaska's figures are distorted by the mid-year Hawaiian acquisition and should be interpreted with caution.

ANSWER: Delta Air Lines appears to have had the most efficient cost structure among the five in FY2024 (lowest operating-expense-to-revenue ratio, ~90.3%, and highest operating margin, ~9.7%), based on a revenue-normalized proxy since true CASM (cost per available seat mile) data was not available in the source filings; this ranking should be treated as approximate given the lack of unit-cost (ASM) data and the non-comparability of Alaska's results due to its mid-2024 Hawaiian Airlines acquisition.
